title: TB9-03523
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss the appeal brought by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Iraq.

The Appellant alleges that he owns a XXXX, and he and his business partner were extorted by a gang with political connections. He alleges that, after the first extortion payment, he decided to sell his XXXX, and he did so in early 2016. He alleges that, after this, he lived more-or-less in hiding until he fled Iraq in XXXX 2016 and brought his claim for protection in Canada.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the claim. The RPD found that the Appellant lacked credibility, that there was no nexus to the Convention, and, in any event, the Appellant had not established a forward-facing risk. The RPD also held that, while the Appellant had established his identity, there were credibility concerns with some of his identity documents

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in determining he lacked credibility because it ignored his reasonable explanations for credibility issues and ignored or improperly assessed documentation. He also argues that documentation establishes his forward-facing risk. He did not submit new evidence, nor did he request an oral hearing.

I find that the determinative issues in this claim are nexus and forward-facing risk. I find that the Appellant has not established a nexus to the Convention and has not established that he faces a section 97 risk, on a balance of probabilities, in the future. I accept, for the purposes of the analysis, that the Appellant owned a business and was extorted, but I find aspects of his claim relating to forward-facing risk are not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. THE ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 There is an exception to this, where the RAD defers to the RPD if the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. I do not find this case falls into the exception. Therefore, I will be looking at whether the RPD's decision was correct.

The RPD dismissed the claim on a number of grounds. Not all of these are determinative. After an independent review of the record, I find the determinative issues are nexus and forward-facing risk. The RPD made credibility findings relating to forward-facing risk, and I will address these in my analysis. However, I am not relying on the RPD's credibility determination: that the Appellant failed to establish that he owned a XXXX or was threatened as a result. I accept, for the purposes of analysis, that the Appellant owned the XXXX and was threatened as a result. I will therefore not address the Appellant's arguments on this point. I will address the issues as follows: (a) The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant has not established that he has a nexus to the Convention; (b) The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant has not established that he has a section 97 risk on a forward-facing basis, on a balance of probabilities; (i) The RPD correctly concluded that threats after the business closed were not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities; (ii) The RPD correctly assessed the situation of the Appellant's business partner; and (iii) The RPD correctly assessed the risk based on the passage of time. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant has not established that he has a nexus to the Convention

The RPD concluded that the Appellant had not established a nexus to the Convention. The RPD concluded that, even if the alleged extortionist was politically connected, there was no link between the extortion and political opinion because the Appellant was targeted based on his wealth rather than any political opinion.2 The Appellant has not challenged this finding, and, reviewing the record, I see no error in it.

The Appellant explained that he was targeted because he was a business owner, and many businesses faced extortion.3 Therefore, I concur with the RPD that the Appellant's claim does not have a nexus to the Convention. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant has not established that he has a section 97 risk on a forward-facing basis, on a balance of probabilities

The RPD concluded that the Appellant had not credibly established that he owned a business and was extorted. In the alternative, the RPD held that the Appellant has not established a forward-facing risk. While I am not relying on the RPD's first conclusion, I agree with the second: the Appellant has not established his forward-facing risk. The RPD correctly concluded that threats after the business closed were not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities

I accept that the Appellant owned a XXXX and that he was extorted as a result and therefore sold his XXXX. However, in considering forward-facing risk, the RPD also considered the credibility of the Appellant's allegations at his hearing that there had been threats after the sale of the XXXX. The RPD found this was not credibly established. I concur.

The RPD considered the Appellant's testimony that, after he sold the XXXX, he heard that someone had come looking for him there and that people were looking for him near where he was living. The RPD found that this lacked credibility because this information was not in the Basis of Claim (BOC) form. The RPD considered that the Appellant filled out his BOC with a lawyer while in detention but found that, if these events occurred, the Appellant would be expected to file an amendment or addendum to his BOC. The Appellant has not challenged this finding, and I see no error in it.

I note that the Appellant's BOC explains that he has had some difficulty filling it out in detention and specifically states: "[b]ecause of these difficult circumstances, I may have to add additional details after submitting this narrative."4 The BOC was filed in December 2016, and the second RPD hearing was in November 2018, almost two years later. No further narrative was filed to address deficiencies in the BOC which were caused by completing the BOC in detention. Therefore, I confirm the RPD's finding.

The RPD also found the evidence that a family member who was a lawyer looked into the Appellant's situation and was subsequently threatened, lacked credibility because the letter from the lawyer was unsigned and because the Appellant had not included this in his BOC. The RPD rejected the explanation, that the Appellant was unaware of this threat, because the lawyer was also a family member and because the assistance allegedly resulted in threats which the RPD expected the writer would have told the Appellant about. The Appellant has not challenged this finding, and I see no reason to disturb it. I further note that, even if the Appellant did not learn of the situation until he received the letter, the letter is dated XXXX XXXX (although no year is on the letter), and it was disclosed in a package on January 19, 2017 indicating it is from 2016, and the Appellant could have amended his BOC to include this information between December 2016 and November 2018. Therefore, I confirm the RPD's finding.

These findings are significant because they are the only allegations of any threats or problems after the Appellant sold the XXXX in early 2016. The RPD correctly assessed the situation of the Appellant's business partner

The RPD considered that the Appellant's business partner remains in Iraq and, in fact, remained in the same city (Sulamaniyah) for some time after the business was sold, and the partner continues to work in a nearby town and live without continued threat. The RPD considered that the business partner was the most similarly situated person to the Appellant and found it significant that he had not experienced problems. The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation that the business partner was at lower risk than him because he was not overtly associated with the business. The RPD found this indicated a lack of forward-facing risk for the Appellant.5
The Appellant argues that this conclusion is erroneous because it ignores the Appellant's circumstances and the evidence. I do not agree.

The Appellant argues that his circumstances are different from the business partner because he is the face of the XXXX, and he spoke personally to the persecutors and gave the money to them as opposed to his partner who was not directly involved.6 He argues that this increases his risk and that the business partner is not safe but simply cannot leave Iraq. I do not find this argument persuasive. The letter from the business partner makes clear that he too was subject to bullying and extortion.7 The RPD considered this and found that the business partner was not in a substantially different position because the evidence was that the business partner was also implicated in the extortion request despite being less public facing. I see no error in this.

The Appellant also argues that the RPD came to this conclusion without considering the report of a researcher who determined that the Appellant's situation is different because it has gone beyond mere finances into the realm of "honour" and therefore puts the Appellant in a different type of risk.8 I note that the report was not put forward as expert evidence, and the researcher, while having a relevant curriculum vitae, is not an accredited expert. Additionally, I reviewed the report of the researcher, and while I find that some of it is persuasive, I do not find that the portion of the report in which the researcher discusses forward-facing risk to be persuasive because it contradicts objective evidence on file.

The researcher states that he feels that the Appellant would be in immediate danger of violent retribution, including the possibility of murder or murder of his family, particularly because the persecutor feels insulted by the Appellant's actions and that this insult brings the matter into the "dangerous realm of 'honour' and is beyond mere finances" as opposed to the situation of the business partner.9 However, objective evidence on honour crimes notes that honour crimes are generally perpetrated against women and that boys and men are "not very likely" to become victims of honour-based violence in Iraqi Kurdistan, and when they do so, most of the time it involves suspected homosexuality.10

The same report notes that honour crimes are usually based on a belief that a family's honour is dependent on the purity of female members and consists of crimes perpetrated by family members against a relative who is "perceived to have brought shame upon the family or tribe."11 The articles also states that honour crimes are "overwhelmingly perpetrated by male family members against female relatives although occasionally males are also the victims of such violence."12 This is mirrored by documents provided to the Board by the Appellant, himself.13

I find that the report's characterization of honour is out of line with the objective documentation. Therefore, I do not find that the report establishes that the Appellant faces a section 97 risk on a forward-facing basis, on a balance of probabilities. The RPD correctly assessed the risk based on the passage of time

The RPD considered that the Appellant sold his business in XXXX 2016 and remained in Iraq until XXXX 2016. The RPD considered that, during this time, the Appellant voluntarily went out to obtain a new identity card which undermines his statement that he avoided being in public. The RPD found that there was a lack of evidence of problems or threats from XXXX to XXXX 2016, which indicates that risk to the Appellant after selling the business is low.14

The Appellant argues that he explained that he believed his risk of doing this was low because it was a public place, and therefore it would be less of a risk.15 I find that the issue of whether the act of obtaining the identity card put the Appellant at risk is not determinative, as the overall evidence does not show any credible threats in the time the Appellant remained in Iraq, as discussed above.

Moreover, the Appellant's claim was rejected in January 2019 over a year and a half ago. In that time, the Appellant has presented no evidence indicating that his family have had any further problems. As noted above, the RPD correctly found that there was no credible evidence to establish threats after XXXX 2016. Therefore, the Appellant has not established with reliable evidence that he or anyone in his family or his business have had any problems in over four years. On this basis, I find that the Appellant has not established a forward-facing risk to his life, of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or of torture, on a balance of probabilities.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Erin Bobkin E.
